stem:
Mia is 20 months old and well. Over the past month her parents have noticed a white glow in her right pupil in several flash photographs. Her red reflex was recorded as normal at her 6-week check. Today the GP cannot obtain a red reflex from the right eye; the left reflex is normal. Her eyes look straight, and there is no redness, fever or trauma.

What is the most appropriate next step for the GP?

options.label: A
options.text: Phone the on-call ophthalmologist for review today
options.explanation: Correct. A newly absent red reflex with a white pupil in photographs needs same-day ophthalmology assessment for causes including retinoblastoma and cataract; the GP should speak to the on-call service.

options.label: B
options.text: Request an orbital ultrasound, then refer with the result
options.explanation: Imaging is for the specialist to choose. Arranging it first delays assessment of a possible retinoblastoma.

options.label: C
options.text: Recheck the red reflex at the 2-year well-child visit
options.explanation: A normal reflex at 6 weeks does not clear a new abnormality: retinoblastoma and cataract can develop later. A confirmed abnormal reflex needs action now.

options.label: D
options.text: Send a routine referral to the eye clinic
options.explanation: A routine appointment is too slow for an unexplained white pupil; the specialist service should be contacted today.

options.label: E
options.text: Refer to a local optometrist within two weeks
options.explanation: A community optometry appointment delays specialist assessment of a potentially sight- or life-threatening lesion.

context: A white pupil or absent red reflex needs immediate ophthalmology assessment for causes including retinoblastoma and cataract.
